audioscript.text: Part 1, you will hear an interview with a woman who is doing a survey on transport.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Excuse me, would you mind if I asked you some questions?
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: We're doing a survey on transport.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: Yes, that's OK.
audioscript.speaker: SADIE

audioscript.text: First of all can I take your name?
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: Yes, it's Sadie Jones.
audioscript.speaker: SADIE

audioscript.text: Thanks very much.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: And could I have your date of birth?
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: Just the year will do, actually.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: Is that all right?
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: Uh. Yes, that's fine.
audioscript.speaker: SADIE

audioscript.text: So, next your post code please.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: It's DW307YZ.
audioscript.speaker: SADIE
audioscript.explain: Q1: The interviewer asks for her postcode, and she directly says *'It's DW307YZ'*. So the answer is **DW307YZ**.

audioscript.text: Great, thanks.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: Is that in Wells?
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: No, it's actually in Harborne.
audioscript.speaker: SADIE

audioscript.text: Wells isn't far from there, though.
audioscript.speaker: SADIE

audioscript.text: I really like that area.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: My grandmother lived there when I was a kid.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: Yes, it is nice.
audioscript.speaker: SADIE

audioscript.text: Right, so now I want to ask you some questions about how you traveled here today.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: Did you use public transport?
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: Yes, I came by bus.
audioscript.speaker: SADIE

audioscript.text: OK, and that was today.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: It's the 24th of April, isn't it?
audioscript.speaker: MAN
audioscript.explain: Q2: The interviewer says *'It's the 24th of April, isn't it?'* and Sadie agrees, saying *'actually you're right'*. So the date is **24 April**.

audioscript.text: Isn't it the 25th uh, no, ha, actually you're right.
audioscript.speaker: SADIE
audioscript.explain: Q2: The interviewer says *'It's the 24th of April, isn't it?'* and Sadie agrees, saying *'actually you're right'*. So the date is **24 April**.

audioscript.text: Ha ha ha.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: And what was the reason for your trip today?
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: I can see you've got some shopping with you.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: Yes, I did some shopping, but the main reason I came here was to go to the dentist.
audioscript.speaker: SADIE
audioscript.explain: Q3: Sadie says she did some shopping, but the *'main reason'* for her trip was *'to go to the dentist'*. So the answer is **dentist**.

audioscript.text: That's not much fun.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: Hope it was nothing serious.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: No, it was just a check-up.
audioscript.speaker: SADIE

audioscript.text: It's fine.
audioscript.speaker: SADIE

audioscript.text: Good.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: Do you normally travel by bus into the city center?
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: Yes, I stopped driving ages ago, because parking was so difficult to find, and it cost so much.
audioscript.speaker: SADIE
audioscript.explain: Q4: She explains she stopped driving because *'parking was so difficult to find, and it cost so much'*. The high cost of **parking** is the reason she now takes the bus.

audioscript.text: I see.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: The bus is much more convenient too. It only takes about 30 minutes.
audioscript.speaker: SADIE

audioscript.text: That's good.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: So where did you start your journey?
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: At the bus stop on Claxby Street.
audioscript.speaker: SADIE
audioscript.explain: Q5: When asked where she started her journey, she says *'At the bus stop on Claxby Street'*. So the answer is **Claxby**.

audioscript.text: Is that CLAXBY?
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: That's right.
audioscript.speaker: SADIE

audioscript.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: And how satisfied with the service are you?
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: Do you have any complaints?
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: Well, as I said, it's very convenient and quick when it's on time.
audioscript.speaker: SADIE

audioscript.text: But this morning it was late, only about 10 minutes, but still.
audioscript.speaker: SADIE
audioscript.explain: Q6: Her complaint is that *'this morning it was late'*. So the bus today was **late**.

audioscript.text: Yes, I understand that's annoying.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: And what about the timetable?
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: Do you have any comments about that?
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: Hmm, I suppose I mainly use the bus during the day, but anytime I've been in town in the evening.
audioscript.speaker: SADIE

audioscript.text: Uh. For dinner or at the cinema.
audioscript.speaker: SADIE

audioscript.text: I've noticed you have to wait a long time for a bus.
audioscript.speaker: SADIE
audioscript.explain: Q7: She says that when she is in town in the *'evening'*, you have to wait a long time for a bus. So the frequency of buses is a problem in the **evening**.

audioscript.text: Uh. There aren't that many.
audioscript.speaker: SADIE
audioscript.explain: Q7: She says that when she is in town in the *'evening'*, you have to wait a long time for a bus. So the frequency of buses is a problem in the **evening**.

audioscript.text: OK, thanks.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: So now, I'd like to ask you about your car use.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: Well, I have got a car, but I don't use it that often.
audioscript.speaker: SADIE

audioscript.text: Mainly just to go to the supermarket.
audioscript.speaker: SADIE
audioscript.explain: Q8: She says she mainly uses her car *'just to go to the supermarket'*. So she goes to the **supermarket** by car.

audioscript.text: But that's about it really.
audioscript.speaker: SADIE

audioscript.text: My husband uses it at the weekends to go to the golf club.
audioscript.speaker: SADIE

audioscript.text: And what about a bicycle?
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: I don't actually have one at the moment.
audioscript.speaker: SADIE

audioscript.text: What about the city bikes you can rent?
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: Do you ever use those?
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: No, I'm not keen on cycling there because of all the pollution.
audioscript.speaker: SADIE
audioscript.explain: Q9: She says she is not keen on cycling in the city *'because of all the pollution'*. So the reason she dislikes it is **pollution**.

audioscript.text: But I would like to get a bike.
audioscript.speaker: SADIE

audioscript.text: It would be good to use it to get to work.
audioscript.speaker: SADIE

audioscript.text: So, why haven't you got one now?
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: Well, I live in a flat on the 2nd floor.
audioscript.speaker: SADIE

audioscript.text: And it doesn't have any storage, so we'd have to leave it in the hall outside the flat.
audioscript.speaker: SADIE
audioscript.explain: Q10: She explains she lives in a flat that *'doesn't have any storage'* for a bike. So the lack of **storage** is why she doesn't own one.

audioscript.text: I see.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: OK, well I think that's all we need from you today...
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: That is the end of part 1.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You now have one minute to check your answers to part 1.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Part 2, you will hear a woman speaking to a group of people who are interested in becoming volunteers for an organization called ACE.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Good evening everyone.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Let me start by welcoming you all to this talk, and thanking you for taking the time to consider joining ACE voluntary organization.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: ACE offers support to people and services in the local area, and we're now looking for more volunteers to help us do this.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: By the way, I hope you're all comfortable.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: We have brought in extra seats so that no one has to stand, but it does mean that the people at the back of the room may be a bit squashed.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q11: The speaker says *'We have brought in extra seats so that no one has to stand, but it does mean that the people at the back of the room may be a bit squashed'*. **'Squashed'** means very close together. So the answer is **C**.

audioscript.text: We'll only be here for about half an hour, so, hopefully, that's OK.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: One of the first questions we're often asked is how old you need to be to volunteer.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Well, you can be as young as 16, or you can be 60 or over.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: It all depends on what type of voluntary work you want to do.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Other considerations such as reliability are crucial in voluntary work.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q12: The passage says *'Other considerations such as reliability are crucial'* and *'age isn't related to these'*. This means **reliability** is more important than **age**. So the answer is **A**.

audioscript.text: And age isn't related to these in our experience.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q12: The passage says *'Other considerations such as reliability are crucial'* and *'age isn't related to these'*. This means **reliability** is more important than **age**. So the answer is **A**.

audioscript.text: Another question we get asked relates to training.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Well, there's plenty of that, and it's all face to face.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: What's more, training doesn't end when you start working for us.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: It takes place before, during, and after periods of work.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q13: The speaker says training *'takes place before, during, and after periods of work'*. This means it never really stops — it is **continuous**. So the answer is **A**.

audioscript.text: Often it's run by other experienced volunteers, as managers tend to prefer to get on with other things.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Now, I would ask you to consider a couple of important issues before you decide to apply for voluntary work.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: We don't worry about why you want to be a volunteer.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: People have many different reasons that range from getting work experience to just doing something they've always wanted to do, but it is critical that you have enough hours in the day.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain:
Q14: The speaker says *'it is critical that you have enough hours in the day'* — **'enough hours'** means your **availability**. Also, *'What we value is dedication'* — **'dedication'** means your **level of commitment**. So the two issues are **B** and **E**.

Q15: The speaker says *'it is critical that you have enough hours in the day'* — **'enough hours'** means your **availability**. Also, *'What we value is dedication'* — **'dedication'** means your **level of commitment**. So the two issues are **B** and **E**.

audioscript.text: For whatever role we agree is suitable for you.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: If being a volunteer becomes stressful, then it's best not to do it at all.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: You may think that your income is important.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: But we don't ask about that.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: It's up to you to decide if you can work without earning money.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: What we value is dedication.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Some of our most loyal volunteers earn very little themselves.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: But still give their full energy to the work they do with us.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: OK, so let's take a look at some of the work areas that we need volunteers for, and the sort of things that would help you in those.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: You may wish simply to help us raise money.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: If you have the creativity to come up with an imaginative or novel way of fundraising, we'd be delighted.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q16: The passage says for fundraising, it helps to have *'creativity to come up with an imaginative or novel way'*. **'Imaginative or novel'** means **original, new ideas**. So the answer is **B**.

audioscript.text: As standing in the local streets or shops with a collection box can be rather boring.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: One outdoor activity that we need volunteers for is litter collection, and for this it's useful if you can walk for long periods, sometimes uphill.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q17: For litter collection, the speaker says *'it's useful if you can walk for long periods, sometimes uphill'*. This means you need **a good level of fitness**. So the answer is **G**.

audioscript.text: Some of our regular collectors are quite elderly, but very active and keen to protect the environment.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: If you enjoy working with children, we have three vacancies for what are called playmates.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: These volunteers help children learn about staying healthy.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Through a range of out of school activities.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: You don't need to have children yourself, but it's good if you know something about nutrition, and can give clear instructions.

audioscript.text: Part 4, you will hear a zoology student giving a presentation on the process of moving wild elephants to a new reserve known as translocation.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: For my presentation today, I want to tell you about how groups of elephants have been moved and settled in new reserves.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: This is known as translocation, and has been carried out in Malawi in Africa in recent years.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The reason this is being done is because of overpopulation of elephants in some areas.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Overpopulation is a good problem to have, and not one we tend to hear about very often, in Malawi's Majete National Park.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The elephant population had been wiped out by poachers who killed the elephants for their ivory, but in 2003 the park was restocked.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And effective law enforcement was introduced.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Since then, not a single elephant has been poached.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: In this safe environment, the elephant population boomed.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Breeding went so well that there were more elephants than the park could support.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: This led to a number of problems.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Firstly, there was more competition for food, which meant that some elephants were suffering from hunger.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: As there was a limit to the amount of food in the national park, some elephants began looking further afield.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Elephants were routinely knocking down fences around the park.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q31: The passage says elephants were *'routinely knocking down fences'* — the question asks about **damage** to something in the park. *'Knocking down'* means **damaging**, so the answer is **fences**.

audioscript.text: Which then had to be repaired at a significant cost.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: To solve this problem, the decision was made to move dozens of elephants from Majete National Park to Nkhotakota Wildlife Park.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Where there were no elephants. But obviously, attempting to move significant numbers of elephants to a new home 300 kilometers away.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Is quite a challenge.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: So, how did this translocation process work in practice?
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Elephants were moved in groups of between eight and 20, all belonging to one family.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q32: The passage says elephants were moved in groups *'all belonging to one family'* — the question asks for a group from the same what. *'Belonging to one'* means from the same group, so the answer is **family**.

audioscript.text: Because relationships are very important to elephants, they all had to be moved at the same time.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: A team of vets and park rangers flew over the park in helicopters, and targeted a group, which were rounded up, and directed to a designated open plain.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q33: The passage says the team *'flew over the park in helicopters'* to round up elephants — the question asks what they used to help guide them. *'Flew over'* means they used them to direct the elephants, so the answer is **helicopters**.

audioscript.text: The vets then used darts to immobilize the elephants.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: This was a tricky maneuver, as they not only had to select the right dose of tranquilizer.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: For different sized elephants, but they had to dart the elephants as they were running around.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: This also had to be done as quickly as possible, so as to minimize the stress caused.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q34: The passage says the darting had to be done quickly *'so as to minimize the stress caused'* — the question asks what they wanted to reduce. *'Minimize'* means **reduce**, so the answer is **stress**.

audioscript.text: As soon as the elephants began to flop onto the ground, the team moved in to take care of them.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: To avoid the risk of suffocation, the team had to make sure none of the elephants were lying on their chests, because their lungs could be crushed in this position.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: So, all the elephants had to be placed on their sides.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q35: The passage says elephants had to be *'placed on their sides'* to avoid lung damage — the question asks how they were turned. *'Placed on'* means they were turned onto them, so the answer is **sides**.

audioscript.text: One person stayed with each elephant, while they waited for the vets to do checks.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: It was very important to keep an eye on their breathing.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q36: The passage says it was *'very important to keep an eye on their breathing'* — the question asks what was monitored constantly. *'Keep an eye on'* means **monitored**, so the answer is **breathing**.

audioscript.text: If there were fewer than 6 breaths per minute, the elephant would need urgent medical attention.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Collars were fitted to the matriarch in each group, so their movements could be tracked in their new home.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Measurements were taken of each elephant's tusks.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Elephants with large tusks would be at greater risk from poachers, and also of their feet.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q37: The passage says measurements were taken of tusks *'and also of their feet'* — the question asks what other data was taken besides tusks. The passage directly mentions it, so the answer is **feet**.

audioscript.text: The elephants were then taken to a recovery area, before being loaded onto trucks and transported to their new home.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The elephants translocated to Nkhotakota settled in very well, and the project has generally been accepted to have been a huge success.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And not just for the elephants.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Employment prospects have improved enormously, contributing to rising living standards for the whole community.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q38: The passage says *'Employment prospects have improved enormously'* — the question asks about what opportunities increased. *'Prospects'* means **opportunities**, so the answer is **employment**.

audioscript.text: Poaching is no longer an issue, as former poachers are able to find more reliable sources of income.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: In fact, many of them volunteered to give up their weapons.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q39: The passage says former poachers *'volunteered to give up their weapons'* — the question asks about a reduction in poachers and what else. *'Give up'* means they stopped having them, so the answer is **weapons**.

audioscript.text: As they were no longer of any use to them.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: More than two dozen elephants have been born at Nkhotakota since relocation. With an area of more than 1,800 square kilometers, there's plenty of space for the elephant population to continue to grow.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Their presence is also helping to rebalance Nkhotakota's damaged ecosystem.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And providing a sustainable conservation model, which could be replicated in other parks.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: All this has been a big draw for tourism, which contributes five times more than the illegal wildlife trade to GDP.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q40: The passage says *'All this has been a big draw for tourism'* which contributes to GDP — the question asks what increased as a contributor. *'Big draw'* means an increase, so the answer is **tourism**.

audioscript.text: And this is mainly because of the elephants.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: There's also been a dramatic rise in interest from...
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: That is the end of part 4.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You now have one minute to check your answers to part 4.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Part 4, you will hear a student on a fashion design course giving a talk about the history of pockets.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Good morning.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Now we've been asked to choose an aspect of European clothing or fashion, and to talk about its development over time.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: I decided to focus on a rather small area of clothing, and that's pockets.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: I chose pockets for two reasons really.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: We all have them in jeans.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Jackets, coats for example, and even though we often carry bags or briefcases as well, nothing is quite as convenient as being able to pop your phone or credit card into your pocket.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q31: The passage says *'nothing is quite as convenient as being able to pop your phone or credit card into your pocket'* — **'convenient'** means easy and useful. So the answer is **convenient**.

audioscript.text: Yet, I suspect that other than that, people don't really think about pockets too much, and they're rather overlooked as a fashion item.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: It's certainly very interesting to go back in time, and see how pockets developed for men and women.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: In the 18th century, fashions were quite different from the way they are now.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Pockets were too.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: If we think about male fashion first, that was the time when suits became popular.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q32: The passage says *'that was the time when suits became popular'* — men started wearing **suits** in the 18th century. So the answer is **suits**.

audioscript.text: Trousers were knee length only, and referred to as breeches.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The waistcoats were short, and the jackets were long, but all three garments were lined with material, and pockets were sewn into this cloth, by whichever tailor the customer used.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q33: The passage says pockets were sewn *'by whichever tailor the customer used'* — a **tailor** is a person who makes clothes. So the answer is **tailor**.

audioscript.text: The wearer could then carry small objects such as pencils or coins on their person, and reach them through a gap in the lining.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Coat pockets became increasingly decorative on the outside for men who wanted to look stylish, but they were often larger, but plainer, if the wearer was someone with a profession who needed to carry medical instruments, a doctor or physician for example.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q34: The passage says bigger pockets were for *'someone with a profession'* like a doctor — **'profession'** means a type of job. So the answer is **profession**.

audioscript.text: The development of women's pockets was a little different.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: For one thing, they weren't nearly as visible or as easy to reach as men's.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q35: The passage says women's pockets *'weren't nearly as visible'* as men's — **'visible'** means easy to see. So the answer is **visible**.

audioscript.text: In the 18th and 19th centuries, women carried numerous possessions on their person, and some of these could be worth a lot of money.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Women were more vulnerable to theft, and wealthy women in particular worried constantly about pickpockets.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: So, what they did was to have a pair of pockets made.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: That were tied together with string.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q36: The passage says the pockets *'were tied together with string'* — **string** is the material used to link them. So the answer is **string**.

audioscript.text: The pockets were made of fabric, which might be recycled cloth if the wearer had little money, or something more expensive.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Such as linen, sometimes featuring very delicate embroidery.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Women tied the pockets around their waist, so that they hung beneath their clothes.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q37: The passage says *'women tied the pockets around their waist'* — the pockets hung from the **waist**. So the answer is **waist**.

audioscript.text: Remember, skirts were long then, and there was plenty of room to hide a whole range of small possessions between the layers of petticoats that were commonly worn.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: They would have an opening in the folds of their skirts, through which they could reach whatever they needed, like their perfume.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q38: The passage says they could reach items *'like their perfume'* through a gap — **perfume** is an example of a small item. So the answer is **perfume**.

audioscript.text: Working women of course, also needed to carry around items that they might use for whatever job or trade they were involved in, but their pairs of pockets still remained on the inside of their clothing.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: They just got bigger or longer, sometimes reaching down to their knees.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: So, the tie-on pockets went well into the 19th century, and only changed when fashion altered towards the end of that period.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: That's when dresses became tighter and less bulky, and the pairs of pockets became very noticeable.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: They stood out too much, and detracted from the woman's image.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q39: The passage says hidden pockets *'detracted from the woman's image'* — they had a bad effect on the **image**. So the answer is **image**.

audioscript.text: Women who had been used to carrying around a range of personal possessions, and still wanted to, needed somewhere to carry these items about their person.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: That was when small bags or pouches as they were known came into fashion, and of course, they inevitably led on to the handbag of more modern times.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q40: The passage says pouches *'led on to the handbag of more modern times'* — women later carried a **handbag**. So the answer is **handbag**.

audioscript.text: Particularly when fashion removed pockets altogether.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: That is the end of part 4.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You now have one minute to check your answers to part 4.

audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: What are the problems in developing such a system?

audioscript.text: Well, for one thing, satellites are relatively cheap these days.

audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q33: The passage mentions *'constellations consisting of thousands of them'* — **'thousands'** is the number. The question says constellations are made up of something of satellites. So the answer is **'thousands'**.

audioscript.text: So while we have international systems for ensuring we know where the planes in our skies are, and to prevent them from colliding with one another.

audioscript.text: And it isn't just entire satellites that we need to consider.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: A greater threat is the huge amount of space debris in orbit around the Earth, broken bits of satellite and junk from space stations and so on.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And some of these are so small that they can be very hard to identify, but they can still be very dangerous.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: In addition, some operators may be unwilling to share information about the satellites they've launched.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: For example, a satellite may be designed for military purposes.

audioscript.explain: Q36: The passage says a satellite *'may be designed for military purposes'* — **'military'** means for the army or war. The question says operators may be unwilling to share details of satellites used for something or commercial reasons. So the answer is **'military'**.

audioscript.text: Or it may have been launched for commercial reasons, and the operators don't want competitors to have information about it, and even if the operators are willing to provide it.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The information isn't easy to collect.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Details are needed about the object itself, as well as about its location at a particular time.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And remember that a satellite isn't very big, and it's likely to be moving at thousands of kilometers an hour.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: We don't have any sensors.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: That can constantly follow something moving so fast, so all that the scientists can do is to put forward a prediction concerning where the satellite is heading next.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q38: The passage says scientists can only *'put forward a prediction'* — **'prediction'** means a guess about the future. The question says scientists can only make a something about where the satellite will go. So the answer is **'prediction'**.

audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: One key issue is the way in which information is dealt with.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: We need more information, but it also needs to be accessible at a global level.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: So we need to establish shared standards that we can all agree on for the way in which this information is presented.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: We already do this in other areas of science.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: So although this is a challenge, it's not an impossible task.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Then as all this information's collected, it needs to be put together so it can be used.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q39: The passage says this will involve *'creating a single database'* — **'database'** is a place to store information on a computer. The question says the information should be combined in one something. So the answer is **'database'**.

audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q40: The passage says the system must be one that *'establishes trust in the people that use it'* — **'trust'** means believing someone is good and honest. The question says a coordinated system must be designed to create something in its users. So the answer is **'trust'**.

audioscript.text: Part 2, you will hear a guide at a farming museum talking to a group of visitors.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Good morning everyone, and welcome to the Museum of Farming Life.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: I understand it's your first visit here, so I'd like to give you some background information about the museum.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And then explain a little about what you can see during your visit.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: So, where we're standing at the moment is the entrance to a large building.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: That was constructed in 1880, as the home of a local businessman, Alfred Palmer, of the Palmer Biscuit Factory.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q11: The passage says the building was *'constructed in 1880, as the home of a local businessman'* — **'home'** means a **private house**. So the answer is **B**.

audioscript.text: It was later sold, and became a hall of residence for students in 1911, and a museum in 1951.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: In 2005, a modern extension was built to accommodate the museum's collections.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The museum's owned by the university, and apart from two rooms that are our offices, the university uses the main part of the building.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: You may see students going into the building for lessons, but it's not open to museum visitors, I'm afraid.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q12: The guide says *'You may see students going into the building for lessons'* — **'lessons'** means **teaching**. So the university uses it as **teaching rooms**, which is **A**.

audioscript.text: It's a shame, because the interior architectural features are outstanding.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Especially the room that used to be the library.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Luckily, we've managed to keep entry to the museum free.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q13: The guide says entry is *'free'* but there is a *'donation box'* and you can *'give whatever amount you consider appropriate'*. This means **visitors decide** if they pay — you are not forced. So the answer is **A**.

audioscript.text: This includes access to all the galleries, outdoor areas, and the rooms for special exhibitions.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: We run activities for children and students, such as the Museum Club, for which there's no charge.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: We do have a donation box just over there, so feel free to give whatever amount you consider appropriate.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q13: The guide says entry is *'free'* but there is a *'donation box'* and you can *'give whatever amount you consider appropriate'*. This means **visitors decide** if they pay — you are not forced. So the answer is **A**.

audioscript.text: We do have a cloakroom.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: If you'd like to leave your coats and bags somewhere.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Unlike other museums, photography is allowed here, so you might like to keep your cameras with you.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: You might be more comfortable not carrying around heavy rucksacks.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q14: The guide says *'You might be more comfortable not carrying around heavy rucksacks'* — **'rucksacks'** are **bags**. So you are advised to leave **bags** in the cloakroom, which is **C**.

audioscript.text: Though keep your coats and jackets on, as it's quite cold in the museum garden today.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: I'd like to tell you about the different areas of the museum.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Just inside and outside the main gallery, we have an area called Four Seasons.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Here, you can watch a four-minute animation of a woodland scene.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: It was designed especially for the museum by a group of young people on a film studies course, and it's beautiful.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q15: The passage says the animation was *'designed especially for the museum by a group of young people on a film studies course'* — this means it was **created by students**. So the answer is **F**.

audioscript.text: Children absolutely love it, but then so do adults.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The main gallery's called Town and Country. It includes a photographic collection of prize-winning sheep and shepherds.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Leaving Town and Country, you enter Farmhouse Kitchen, which is... well, self-explanatory.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Here we have the oldest collection of equipment for making butter and cheese in the country.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And this morning, a specialist cheesemaker will be giving demonstrations of how it's produced.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q16: The guide says *'a specialist cheesemaker will be giving demonstrations'* — a **'specialist'** is an **expert**. So an **expert is here today**, which is **G**.

audioscript.text: You may even get to try some.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: After that, you can go in two directions.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: To the right is a staircase that takes you up to a landing, from where you can look down on the galleries.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: To the left is a room called A Year on the Farm.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: There is lots of seating here, as sometimes we use the room for school visits, so it's a good place to stop for a rest.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: If you're feeling competitive, you can take our memory test, in which you answer questions about things you've seen in the museum.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q17: The passage mentions a *'memory test, in which you answer questions about things you've seen'* — a **'test'** with questions is a **quiz**. So there is a **quiz for visitors**, which is **E**.

audioscript.text: The next area is called Wagon Walk.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: This contains farm carts from nearly every part of the country.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: It's surprising how much regional variation there was.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Beside the carts are display boards with information about each one.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Part 4, you will hear a literature student giving a talk about Victor Hugo, a famous 19th century French writer.

audioscript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: The person I've chosen to talk about is the French writer Victor Hugo.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Many people have heard of him because his novel, Les Miserables,
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: which he wrote in 1862, is famous around the world.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: It became a stage musical in the 1980s, and a film version was also released in 2012.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: So some of us, I'm sure, have a pretty general idea of the plot, but we know much less about the author.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q31: The passage says we have *'a pretty general idea of the plot, but we know much less about the author'*. The question asks what we know more about than the author — that is the **'plot'**. So the answer is **plot**.

audioscript.text: Today, I'm going to provide a little more insight into this talented man.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And I'm going to talk particularly about the home he had on the island of Guernsey in the British Channel Islands, but first, his early career.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: As I've said, he was a writer.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: He was at the height of his career in Paris, and he was very highly regarded by his colleagues.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: As far as literature was concerned, he was the leading figure of the Romantic movement.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: However, as well as being a literary genius, he also gave many speeches about issues like the level of poverty in his society.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q32: The passage says he gave speeches about *'issues like the level of poverty in his society'*. The question lists social issues he spoke about — **'poverty'** is one of them, along with education. So the answer is **poverty**.

audioscript.text: He felt very strongly about this, and about other areas where change was needed, like education.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: This kind of outspoken criticism was not well liked by the rulers of France.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And eventually the emperor - Napoleon III - told Victor Hugo to leave Paris and not return.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: In other words, he sent him into exile.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: So Victor Hugo was forced to reside in other parts of Europe.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q33: The passage says Victor Hugo *'was forced to reside in other parts of Europe'*. **'Reside'** means **'live'** — the question says he had to *'live elsewhere in'* somewhere. That place is **Europe**. So the answer is **Europe**.

audioscript.text: Guernsey was actually his third place of exile.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And he landed there in 1855.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: He produced a lot while on Guernsey, including Les Miserables.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And to do this, he had to spend a great deal of time in the home that he had there.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: This was a property that he bought using the money he'd made in France, from the publication of a collection of his poetry.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q34: The passage says he bought the house using money *'from the publication of a collection of his poetry'*. The question asks what he sold to get income — it was his **'poetry'**. So the answer is **poetry**.

audioscript.text: It was the only property he ever owned, and he was very proud of it.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The property Victor Hugo bought on Guernsey was a large five-storey house in the capital town of St Peter Port, and he lived there for 15 years.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Returning to France in 1870 when Napoleon's empire collapsed.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: He decorated and furnished each level or floor of the house in unique and wonderful ways, and many people consider the inside of the house to be a work of art.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Today, it's a museum that attracts 200,000 visitors a year.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: He lived in the house with his family, and portraits of its members still hang in rooms on the ground floor, along with drawings that he did during his travels.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q35: The passage says the ground floor has *'portraits... along with drawings that he did during his travels'*. The question lists three things on the ground floor: portraits, something, and tapestries. That something is **'drawings'**. So the answer is **drawings**.

audioscript.text: That he felt were important to him.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: In other ground floor rooms, there are huge tapestries that he would have designed and loved.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The walls are covered in dark wood panelling that Victor Hugo created himself using wooden furniture that he bought in the market.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q36: The passage says he created wall carvings *'using wooden furniture that he bought in the market'*. The question says he bought cheap something made of wood — that something is **'furniture'**. So the answer is **furniture**.

audioscript.text: The items were relatively inexpensive, and he used them to create intricate carvings.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: They gave an atmosphere on the lower level that was shadowy,
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: and rather solemn.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: On the next level of the house, there are two impressive lounges where he entertained his guests.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: One lounge has entirely red furnishings.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Such as sofas and wall coverings, and the other blue.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: There's a strong Chinese influence in these areas, in things like the wallpaper pattern.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q37: The passage says there is a Chinese influence in *'the wallpaper pattern'* and *'the lamps'*. The question asks what has a Chinese design along with wallpaper — that is **'lamps'**. So the answer is **lamps**.

audioscript.text: And the lamps, which he would have made himself by copying original versions.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q37: The passage says there is a Chinese influence in *'the wallpaper pattern'* and *'the lamps'*. The question asks what has a Chinese design along with wallpaper — that is **'lamps'**. So the answer is **lamps**.

audioscript.text: His library, where he left many of his favorite books, forms the hallway to the third floor, and was a comfortable area where he could relax and enjoy his afternoons.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And then, at the very top of the house, there's a room called the Lookout,
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q38: The passage says the top room is called the Lookout *'because it looks out over the harbor'*. The question asks what the room had a view of — it was the **'harbor'** (or **'harbour'**). So the answer is **harbor**.

audioscript.text: called that because it looks out over the harbor.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q38: The passage says the top room is called the Lookout *'because it looks out over the harbor'*. The question asks what the room had a view of — it was the **'harbor'** (or **'harbour'**). So the answer is **harbor**.

audioscript.text: In contrast to the rather dark lower levels, it's full of light, and was like a glass office where he would write until lunchtime.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Often at his desk.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: So Victor Hugo was a man of many talents, but he was also true to his values.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: While living in his house on Guernsey.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: He entertained many other famous writers, but he also invited a large group of local children from the deprived areas of the island to dinner once a week.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q39: The passage says he invited *'a large group of local children from the deprived areas'* to dinner. The question says he entertained poor someone — **'deprived'** means **'poor'**, so those people are **'children'**. So the answer is **children**.

audioscript.text: What's more, he served them their food, which was an extraordinary gesture for the time period.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: In 1927, the house was owned by his relatives, and they decided to donate it to the city of Paris.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q40: The passage says *'the house was owned by his relatives, and they decided to donate it'*. The question asks who gave ownership to Paris — it was his **'relatives'**. So the answer is **relatives**.

audioscript.text: It has since been restored using photographs from the period, and as I mentioned earlier, is now a museum that is open to the public.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: That is the end of part 4.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER
